query: Consider the following context: High-entropy alloys (HEAs) exhibit excellent properties such as high strength, good ductility, superior corrosion resistance, and thermal stability, making them highly promising for applications in the aerospace, energy, and automotive industries. Among them, the FeNiCrMn HEA demonstrates outstanding corrosion resistance while eliminating the expensive Co element present in the “Cantor” alloy, significantly reducing costs. However, current research on the FeNiCrMn HEA has primarily focused on its corrosion resistance, with relatively limited studies on its mechanical properties. In that context, which method can be used for the stated problem, and why?

generation.hypothesis: Using advanced in situ mechanical testing (combining digital image correlation with synchrotron X-ray microscopy) on FeNiCrMn HEA samples will reveal real-time deformation and failure mechanisms—such as dislocation activities, phase transformations, or grain boundary responses—that are not captured by post‐mortem analysis and may correlate with improved mechanical performance under service-like conditions.
generation.material_initial_state: FeNiCrMn high-entropy alloy produced in the as-synthesized or heat-treated state, noted primarily for its excellent corrosion resistance and cost benefits (by eliminating Co).
generation.intervention: Application of an advanced in situ mechanical testing protocol that couples digital image correlation (DIC) with synchrotron X-ray microscopy during mechanical loading.
generation.conditions: Mechanical testing under service-relevant conditions (e.g., room and moderately elevated temperatures) with controlled strain rates to simulate aerospace, energy, and automotive environments.
generation.structural_mediator: Real-time microstructural evolution such as dislocation motion, phase transitions, or grain boundary modifications captured by high-resolution imaging during deformation.
generation.mechanism: The in situ approach will allow direct observation of the initiation and evolution of deformation mechanisms (e.g., slip, twinning, or phase transformation) which govern the material’s mechanical strength and ductility, thereby linking microstructural changes to macroscopic mechanical performance.
generation.predicted_outcome: Distinct, observable microstructural events that correlate with load-induced strains and mechanical responses; these events (e.g., dislocation pile-ups or phase changes) would provide insights into the superior or altered mechanical behavior of the HEA compared to traditional post-mortem analyses.
generation.baseline: Mechanical property evaluations of FeNiCrMn HEA using conventional ex situ testing methods that assess only the final state after deformation.
generation.boundary: Outcomes might be constrained by the resolution limits of the synchrotron imaging and the specific processing history (as-cast versus heat-treated) of the alloy; extreme conditions or high strain rates might also limit the ability to capture all mechanisms in real time.
generation.uncertainty: The extent and precise magnitude of observable microstructural changes during deformation are uncertain and may vary with testing conditions; additional studies would be required to quantify the contributions of each mechanism to the overall mechanical performance.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare FeNiCrMn HEA samples under controlled synthesis (as-cast and heat-treated). Subject samples to in situ mechanical tests using a setup integrating digital image correlation with synchrotron X-ray microscopy while applying controlled loading conditions. Continuously record load-displacement data alongside real-time imaging to capture microstructural changes.
measurements: High-resolution strain maps via digital image correlation
Synchrotron-based X-ray diffraction or imaging data capturing dislocation dynamics and phase changes
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the in situ testing fails to reveal any distinguishable or time-correlated microstructural evolution (such as dislocation motion, twinning, or phase transformation) during mechanical loading that differs from static, ex situ analysis, or if the observed events do not correlate with the mechanical property variations measured, then the hypothesis is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: Refractory high-entropy alloys (HEAs) have excellent mechanical properties, which could make them the substitutes of some superalloys. However, the high melting point of refractory HEAs leads to processing problems when using traditional processing techniques. In this study, a single BCC solid solution of NbMoTaW alloy was formed by selective laser melting (SLM) with a linear energy density of up to 2.83 J/mm. The composition distribution was analyzed, and the element with a lower melting point and lower density showed a negative deviation (no more than 5%) of the molar ratio in the formed alloy. The HEA shows an excellent microstructure, microhardness, and corrosion resistance performance compared with traditional superalloys, making it a new substitute metal with great application prospects in aerospace and energy fields.

Unlike other conventional alloys based on a “principal element,” high-entropy alloy (HEA) is a unique material that maintains a random solid solution structure without forming intermetallic compounds in operating temperatures due to its high configurational entropy [1] – [3] . It also has outstanding physical and chemical properties, which makes it a potential replacement for traditional metallic materials, and it has recently been referred to as a multi-principal element alloy (MPEA) or compositionally concentrated alloy (CCA) [4] – [9] .

As attention in HEAs increases, many studies have been conducted to explore its mechanical, physical and chemical properties [10] – [15] . In particular, equiatomic CoCrFeMnNi HEA, which was the first developed HEA, is the most studied because of its excellent combination of tensile strength and elongation along with excellent fracture toughness and corrosion resistance [6] , [16] – [21] . However, despite the advantages of equiatomic CoCrFeMnNi HEA, many issues arise owing to its low yield strength and costly and complex thermomechanical processing (i.e., multiple casting → hot rolling → homogenization → cold rolling → annealing → cutting, etc.
